## Reduction

The uncovered squares form a permutation matrix, so the covered squares are the grid minus n cells, one in each row and column. The tiles must partition those covered squares into rectangles, and the task is to minimise the number of rectangles.

## Lower bound (sketch)

Count tile corners over the lattice points. Each uncovered square has four corners, and at each such corner the tiles must have at least one corner point. This gives roughly 4n corner incidences. Each uncovered square sitting in a grid corner removes one of these, and at most two grid corners can hold uncovered squares, since they must lie in different rows and columns. Counting the covered grid corners as well yields 4t ≥ 4n + 4 − 2c, where c ≤ 2 is the number of uncovered corner squares. For c ≤ 1 this gives t ≥ n + 1.

The case c = 2 would only allow t ≥ n, and I did not rule it out in general. For n = 2025 I have not verified that it fails, so the lower bound is not fully proved.

## Small cases

- n = 1: 0 tiles.
- n = 2: 2 tiles.
- n = 3: 4 tiles. An exhaustive check over the permutation types shows 3 tiles is impossible.
- n = 4: 5 tiles. Uncovered squares at (1,2), (2,4), (3,1), (4,3) allow a pinwheel of five tiles: one central 2×2 block and four dominoes around it. A case check rules out 4 tiles for the permutations with c ≤ 1, and for the c = 2 permutations I checked.

This matches n + 1 for n = 3 and n = 4.

## Conclusion

The pattern n + 1 holds for the small cases I checked. For n = 2025 this gives 2026. I did not produce an explicit general construction achieving n + 1 for all odd n, so the value 2026 rests on this pattern and the lower-bound count rather than a complete proof.

ANSWER: 2026
